item.title: NASA Mars rover and orbiter suffer glitches
item.description: It's been a bad few weeks for technology on and off the planet, as NASA reported problems with its Perseverance Mars rover and Odyssey orbiter this week. For Perseverance, the problem seems to be a relatively straightforward communications issue that has paused science operations because of low data rates. The Odyssey orbiter, however, is facing an issue that could end the mission. The 2001 Mars Odyssey reached orbit around Mars in October 2001 to search for evidence of water and ice on the surface. The mission was supposed to last two and a half years, but the spacecraft's operations have been extended for a quarter of a century. In that time, it has had its fair share of ups and downs, including the failure of one of its four reaction wheels in 2013. Three reaction wheels are needed to orient the spacecraft; otherwise, it must fall back to its hydrazine thrusters. Earlier in November, between the 4th and 6th, Odyssey dropped into safe mode, which engineers determined was caused by one of the remaining reaction wheels stopping spinning. Science data stopped flowing as the team worked to recover the component; the good news was that the wheel moved when commanded. The bad news is that if the thrusters need to be used, only a few months of fuel remain. More bad news is that the spacecraft is part of NASA's Mars Relay Network, and was responsible for sending back the first post-landing images from the Phoenix lander and the Spirit, Opportunity, and Curiosity rovers. Its loss (should it come to that) would therefore be keenly felt. In the event the orbiter is indeed approaching the end of the road, the European Space Agency's Mars Express (MEX) and Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) could pick up some of the load although, as a former ESA insider put it: "MEX is a science mission that can do relay where TGO is a relay mission that also does science." According to NASA, TGO already sends the most relay data from Mars to Earth. The challenge facing the Perseverance trundlebot is one of communication. On October 30, the rover's main computer detected problems with the primary radio (a series of "heartbeats" from the device did not arrive as expected) and automatically switched to a redundant backup, placing itself in a protective safe mode. So far, so expected. Engineers brought the rover back from safe mode, analyzed the data, and made an unpleasant discovery. The backup radio was not performing as it should – it was operating at approximately half of its expected power output. Both radios were therefore deemed inoperable – at least until the team has got to the bottom of the issues – and the rover has used X-band communications over its high-gain antenna to talk to Earth ever since. The problem here is that the connection provides a significantly lower data rate, meaning science and instrument operations are on hold. Engineers are working first to return the backup radio to operational status, then to address the primary. ®

item.title: ‘The doom of humanity’: will the quest to make robotic hands render us obsolete?
item.description: The one thing stopping AI taking over the world – or at least everyone’s jobs? Dexterity. Human hands are anatomical marvels that engineers have struggled for years to replicate. Experts are racing to change that Just outside Luton, in an Amazon warehouse the size of four football pitches, yellow shelving units pirouette in a digitally choreographed dance. Tubs containing a Lego Spider-Man kit, followed by dishwasher tablets, followed by a pouch of muscle building protein powder whiz along conveyor belts, until they arrive at a human being tasked with stacking the shelving unit that has come to a stop in front of their workstation. This, Amazon says, is the “symphony of people and technology” to which the retail giant owes its success. Following a barrage of negative publicity about working practices, Amazon began to open up its fulfilment centres to carefully controlled free public tours a decade ago. Our guide tells us about the competitive rates of pay Amazon workers receive, their pensions, dental cover and options for flexible working. Her delivery is somewhat robotic. Continue reading...

item.title: Amazon's split personality: AWS embraces bot commerce while main site enforces bans
item.description: Amazon is of two minds when it comes to automated purchasing. The ecommerce giant has been busy banning AI shopping agents from accessing its website. Meanwhile, AWS Marketplace has opened its door to bot-based buying. "Buying software and data through AWS Marketplace just got easier, for you and for the AI agents working alongside you," said Mya Papolu, product marketing manager for AWS Marketplace and Partner Services at Amazon Web Services, in a blog post this week. "For re:Invent 2026, we’re launching capabilities designed to reduce friction across the buying journey." For a company that has blocked bots from Google, Meta, and OpenAI, and sued Perplexity to keep its AI-encumbered Comet browser away, the openness of AWS Marketplace to agentic commerce invites questions. We asked Amazon to explain but we've not heard back. AWS Marketplace is allowing AI agents to scour its site and buy some cloud software products using the x402 agentic payment protocol , which is supported by Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments. Introduced by Coinbase and Cloudflare , x402 got handed over to the Linux Foundation earlier this year, and now has support from a variety of tech platforms, including AWS, Google, Stripe, and various blockchain networks. About a week ago, Brave Software announced support for x402 payments through its search API. AWS requires sellers to register with AWS Marketplace and to integrate the AWS Marketplace x402 SDK to enable agentic product purchases. Transactions settle in USD through AWS billing so existing spending controls can be applied. And now, customers in the US can buy some AWS Marketplace software without an AWS account; instead they're asked to provide an email or social media login, and a credit card. While AWS Marketplace today lists mainly familiar software categories (Business Applications, Data & Analytics, DevOps, Infrastructure Software, and so on), AWS has a broader product inventory in mind. Beyond software and APIs, the biz sees a future in selling content and data. Papolu announced that AWS is now selling " data as a service ." "Data providers can list their offerings in AWS Marketplace, making commercial data accessible to both human teams and the agents working alongside them via the AWS Marketplace website, APIs, and MCP server," she said. This includes services like Moody's Credit MCP server for financial research; Reuters Geopolitical News for AI-structured reporting; US Building Permits, Contractors & Residents Data from Shovels; and US-EN Multi-Speaker Conversational Acoustic Corpus from Uber AI Solutions. In canned remarks provided to AWS, Nandhan Puppala, general manager at Uber AI Solutions, said that data quality and readiness can help advance AI products. Agent mode for AWS Marketplace has been available for about a year as a way to query the market via prompt. That's being expanded to allow deeper queries about seller security and project requirements. Science fiction writer William Gibson's oft-cited line

item.title: PHP 8.6: Things are gonna get a lot more strict around here
item.description: On Thursday, PHP version 8.6 was released on its usual yearly schedule, popping up as if the web scripting language hadn’t been under intense scrutiny this past month. For those who missed it: a swarm of unearthed vulnerabilities has plagued PHP since October, allowing unauthenticated attackers to crash PHP workers or execute arbitrary code on the server. Users of every PHP-based application, including WordPress, Laravel, and Symfony, had to scramble to update their PHP instances. The PHP core development community, along with the PHP Foundation , responded with a coordinated release of patched versions of PHP ( 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, 8.2.36 and the new 8.6) that closed seven critical remote code execution (RCE) flaws in one sweep. In addition to patching specific exploitable holes in the PHP engine, the new version of PHP also tamps down some of PHP’s historically liberal configuration settings. Lucky for PHP, and for the rest of us, core developer Jörg Sowa called out these lax settings in June, when he posted a proposal to set more security-friendly defaults. Sowa saw that three configuration settings of PHP’s session extension – Strict Mode, HttpOnly, and SameSite – were designed to boost security but shipped “with defaults that leave applications unnecessarily exposed.” No cookies for impostors In a retrospective posted last month, the PHP Foundation admitted that consensus-driven gridlock had stalled complex fixes for months and vowed to get patches out the door sooner, should the vulnerabilities leak ahead of the agreed-upon deadline . Code-wise, Sowa’s proposal to harden PHP settings was accepted for PHP 8.6. These changes won’t stop the flood of AI-generated CVEs, but at least these holes will be more difficult to exploit. For Strict Mode, PHP will no longer accept uninitialized session IDs that it didn’t create itself. Before, an attacker could just plant a made-up session ID on the victim to gain entry. “The built-in files handler checks whether a session file for that ID exists on disk; because an attacker-planted ID has no corresponding file, a fresh random ID is generated instead,” Sowa wrote. Furthermore, PHP will now, by default, add the HttpOnly flag to its session Set-Cookie header, blocking client-side JavaScript from reading the session ID, which could otherwise be stolen to masquerade as the user. Believe it or not, any script on the page could read it before. Finally, the server will withhold session cookies on cross-site POST requests, as well as for subrequests and iframes. “Without it, a forged form or link on an attacker-controlled site can trigger authenticated requests using the victim’s session,” Sowa wrote. Going forward, cookies will only be sent on same-site requests and top-level GET navigations, such as clicking a normal link. item.dc:creator: Joab Jackson
item.content:encoded: On Thursday, PHP version 8.6 was released on its usual yearly schedule, popping up as if the web scripting language hadn’t been under intense scrutiny this past month. For those who missed it: a swarm of unearthed vulnerabilities has plagued PHP since October, allowing unauthenticated attackers to crash PHP workers or execute arbitrary code on the server. Users of every PHP-based application, including WordPress, Laravel, and Symfony, had to scramble to update their PHP instances. The PHP core development community, along with the PHP Foundation , responded with a coordinated release of patched versions of PHP ( 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, 8.2.36 and the new 8.6) that closed seven critical remote code execution (RCE) flaws in one sweep. In addition to patching specific exploitable holes in the PHP engine, the new version of PHP also tamps down some of PHP’s historically liberal configuration settings. Lucky for PHP, and for the rest of us, core developer Jörg Sowa called out these lax settings in June, when he posted a proposal to set more security-friendly defaults. Sowa saw that three configuration settings of PHP’s session extension – Strict Mode, HttpOnly, and SameSite – were designed to boost security but shipped “with defaults that leave applications unnecessarily exposed.” No cookies for impostors In a retrospective posted last month, the PHP Foundation admitted that consensus-driven gridlock had stalled complex fixes for months and vowed to get patches out the door sooner, should the vulnerabilities leak ahead of the agreed-upon deadline . Code-wise, Sowa’s proposal to harden PHP settings was accepted for PHP 8.6. These changes won’t stop the flood of AI-generated CVEs, but at least these holes will be more difficult to exploit. For Strict Mode, PHP will no longer accept uninitialized session IDs that it didn’t create itself. Before, an attacker could just plant a made-up session ID on the victim to gain entry. “The built-in files handler checks whether a session file for that ID exists on disk; because an attacker-planted ID has no corresponding file, a fresh random ID is generated instead,” Sowa wrote. Furthermore, PHP will now, by default, add the HttpOnly flag to its session Set-Cookie header, blocking client-side JavaScript from reading the session ID, which could otherwise be stolen to masquerade as the user. Believe it or not, any script on the page could read it before. Finally, the server will withhold session cookies on cross-site POST requests, as well as for subrequests and iframes. “Without it, a forged form or link on an attacker-controlled site can trigger authenticated requests using the victim’s session,” Sowa wrote. Going forward, cookies will only be sent on same-site requests and top-level GET navigations, such as clicking a normal link. Collectively, these changes should thwart session hijacking and cross-site request forgeries. They won’t stop remote code execution hacks, though they will make it a lot more difficult for attackers to gain entry. The new release brings some other security-minded changes as well. The PHP engine will be a lot stricter when it encounters strings with null values (“\0”). In many cases, it will now throw an error rather than silently letting it pass. Null values are a favored trick for triggering RCEs. A C function will treat the null value as the end of the string, processing everything before the null byte and ignoring everything after, much to an attacker’s delight . Continuing in this spirit of “if you see something, say something,” a number of other PHP functions will also no longer remain silent when things go awry. Operations for closing a file or copying data, for instance, will explicitly return a false value when terminating prematurely or failing, an alert developers could use to minimize data integrity bugs. Beyond security, PHP 8.6 also comes with a number of new goodies. PHPers are abuzz over Partial Function Application (PFA), which will let them pre-fill some of a function’s arguments to generate a reusable closure on the fly — leapfrogging JavaScript in this ability. The new edition also gets a native polling API, which will be handy for event-driven networking; a stopwatch-like Duration class that can track elapsed time across more than 250 years; and a clamp() function to ensure a given value stays within an acceptable range. Another tricky day for PHP devs For administrators, this PHP update round may be a bit of a shambles. As backend software engineer Rajekevin Dourepoulle notes in a blog post , these changes will take effect post-installation only if the configurations aren’t specified elsewhere, such as in an application, framework, or even another php.ini file – all of which can override the PHP settings themselves. “In practice: if your deployment reuses the old php.ini (an Ansible template, a COPY php.ini in a Dockerfile, a file copied from server to server), you move to 8.6 and gain nothing, because the explicit session.use_strict_mode = 0 line overrides the new default,” he wrote. Despite all these heroic efforts, PHP remains the champion of inscrutability . ®

item.title: Trump FCC declares California isn't allowed to enforce phone service rules
item.description: The Federal Communications Commission ordered California to stop enforcing its Carrier of Last Resort (COLR) rules against AT&T, setting up another battle between the Trump administration and California over the state's right to enforce its own telecom laws and regulations. AT&T's status as a Carrier of Last Resort in California requires it to offer telephone service to any potential customer in its territory. AT&T wants to stop offering basic phone service to new customers and discontinue service for 184,000 residential customers and 15,000 business customers on June 1, 2027. The order released today granted AT&T's request to preempt state rules, following up on the FCC's previous approval of AT&T's petition to discontinue service. AT&T had tried to achieve the same result in court, but a federal judge rejected its request to override California's rules in July. Read full article Comments

item.title: SpaceX's Starshield troubles in Ukraine could threaten its broader military business
item.description: The representative in the US House expected to chair the House Intelligence Committee in January, Jim Himes (D-Conn.), has threatened to withhold support for funding government-owned systems from SpaceX amid the ongoing inquiry into the use of Starshield in Ukraine. "SpaceX's potentially unilateral modification of a U.S. Government contract, combined with its lack of responsiveness to congressional oversight, calls into question every contract the U.S. Government has with SpaceX," Himes wrote in a letter to SpaceX founder Elon Musk on Friday. CNN first reported the letter's existence. The network also reported that Himes sent a classified communication to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton with a similar message that it would be difficult for Congress to authorize funding for systems with SpaceX as the primary vendor. Read full article Comments

item.title: Google rolls out new search homepage with AI chat history and no search button
item.description: Google's flagship search experience is evolving into an AI experience with stunning speed. Even time-tested elements of search are getting AI makeovers, and the latest to get this treatment is the search homepage on Google.com. A redesign that's been in testing for the last few weeks is now official, bringing easier access to AI chats and dropping the dedicated search button entirely. Google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the new desktop search page after a successful test. The page will now have a few more buttons under the search bar, all connected to AI features. There's an image generation button, one for analyzing files, and one for brainstorming with Gemini. The "I'm Feeling Lucky" button remains, but the Google Search button that used to sit next to it is gone. The search button has obviously been a part of Google's search page forever. However, it wasn't in a very convenient location in the modern interface. When you begin typing a query, the autocomplete suggestions cover that button. You have to click out of the text field to access the button, which is an extra step compared to simply mashing the Enter key to run your search. Read full article Comments

item.title: Meta reconsiders 2030 net-zero goal amid record emissions from AI data centers
item.description: Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Big Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers. The company’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.” “We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report. Read full article Comments

item.title: Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day of trading
item.description: The Nasdaq lost trillions in value, with the AI startup’s IPO failing to buoy it as investors question huge sums being poured into AI buildout Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn? As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory. Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal. Continue reading...

item.title: Visa, Mastercard theft included info useful for phishing, but not draining bank accounts, say researchers
item.description: Visa and Mastercard customer info leaked by the data thieves and extortionists who claim to have stolen it from the financial giants doesn’t include card numbers, passwords, or home addresses. On Thursday, Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase confirmed to The Register that they are investigating third-party breaches that may involve customer information. Ransomware and extortion crew n0n claimed to be responsible for all three, and on Thursday published samples of the stolen files – data-theft groups typically leak some of the compromised data ahead of the official extortion deadline in an effort to put more pressure on victim companies to pay the ransom demand. Researchers at SOCRadar, a threat-intelligence firm that has been tracking n0n since it emerged in September, have parsed all 14 files in the n0n’s published Visa and Mastercard archives, and told us that the files don’t contain any financial details belonging to banking customers. “We found no card numbers, expiry dates, CVVs, passwords, dates of birth, or home addresses in any file,” Ensar Seker, SOCRadar chief information security officer, told The Register . “Visa's statement that no card numbers were affected matches our scan.” Mastercard previously said that stolen data included a “limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information” from a subset of cardholders in a benefits program. According to SOCRadar’s analysis, the leaked files do contain mobile numbers, Bank Identification Number (BIN) prefixes, and dated airline, hotel, and restaurant bookings. So while the data doesn’t include card or account numbers that crooks could use to drain customers' bank accounts or rack up massive credit card bills, “that detail is what a fraudster needs to pose as a concierge desk or a bank,” in an email or voice-phishing social engineering attack, Seker said. It’s also worth noting that the published files only represent about 0.4 percent of the data n0n claims to have hoovered up in the breach: about 4.3 GB and 1.9 million marketing events. “So a further release is possible,” according to Seker. Plus, both datasets come from the same upstream provider, we’re told. They use the same 27-column booking layout, placeholder text, and CRM ID format, Seker said, noting that the most recent record in each stops 69 seconds apart on Oct 26. “This looks like two card programs run on one provider's platform,” he said. “The pattern looks like a batch copy from a marketing and reporting store.” Customer data has left the building The security shop hasn’t analyzed the Chase customer data that n0n also claimed to have published. All three financial firms attributed the compromises to a third-party provider, and while nothing in the stolen files name the vendor, the timing matches up with a Qubole supply-chain campaign disclosed earlier this month by Wiz, working with Google's Mandiant incident responders and AI data security company Sentra. item.dc:creator: Jessica Lyons
item.content:encoded: Visa and Mastercard customer info leaked by the data thieves and extortionists who claim to have stolen it from the financial giants doesn’t include card numbers, passwords, or home addresses. On Thursday, Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase confirmed to The Register that they are investigating third-party breaches that may involve customer information. Ransomware and extortion crew n0n claimed to be responsible for all three, and on Thursday published samples of the stolen files – data-theft groups typically leak some of the compromised data ahead of the official extortion deadline in an effort to put more pressure on victim companies to pay the ransom demand. Researchers at SOCRadar, a threat-intelligence firm that has been tracking n0n since it emerged in September, have parsed all 14 files in the n0n’s published Visa and Mastercard archives, and told us that the files don’t contain any financial details belonging to banking customers. “We found no card numbers, expiry dates, CVVs, passwords, dates of birth, or home addresses in any file,” Ensar Seker, SOCRadar chief information security officer, told The Register . “Visa's statement that no card numbers were affected matches our scan.” Mastercard previously said that stolen data included a “limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information” from a subset of cardholders in a benefits program. According to SOCRadar’s analysis, the leaked files do contain mobile numbers, Bank Identification Number (BIN) prefixes, and dated airline, hotel, and restaurant bookings. So while the data doesn’t include card or account numbers that crooks could use to drain customers' bank accounts or rack up massive credit card bills, “that detail is what a fraudster needs to pose as a concierge desk or a bank,” in an email or voice-phishing social engineering attack, Seker said. It’s also worth noting that the published files only represent about 0.4 percent of the data n0n claims to have hoovered up in the breach: about 4.3 GB and 1.9 million marketing events. “So a further release is possible,” according to Seker. Plus, both datasets come from the same upstream provider, we’re told. They use the same 27-column booking layout, placeholder text, and CRM ID format, Seker said, noting that the most recent record in each stops 69 seconds apart on Oct 26. “This looks like two card programs run on one provider's platform,” he said. “The pattern looks like a batch copy from a marketing and reporting store.” Customer data has left the building The security shop hasn’t analyzed the Chase customer data that n0n also claimed to have published. All three financial firms attributed the compromises to a third-party provider, and while nothing in the stolen files name the vendor, the timing matches up with a Qubole supply-chain campaign disclosed earlier this month by Wiz, working with Google's Mandiant incident responders and AI data security company Sentra. In that attack, which the threat hunters said began on October 14, cybercrims used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account to access dozens of downstream-customers’ environments, stealing secrets and other sensitive data from S3 buckets. N0n also claimed to have carried out this attack. “The timing fits the Qubole supply-chain campaign,” Seker said, adding that this is his company’s assessment, not a confirmed finding. "If it's right, Qubole would be the access path rather than the holder of the data, and the files point to a concierge-services operator behind the brands.” Qubole’s parent company Idera did not respond to The Register ’s inquiries. The financial institutions declined to answer our questions about which provider(s) was compromised in the breach, and whether Qubole was the access path by which their customers’ data was exposed.®

item.title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
item.description: Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve. The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model. Security breaches, prompt theft, and privacy violations To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible. Read full article Comments

item.title: Signal slams door on prying AI agents to protect privacy
item.description: Signal, the encrypted messaging app, has barred Google Gemini, Apple Siri, and other AI agents from accessing messages unless the user has explicitly granted permission, based on privacy concerns. Citing the screenshot blocking implemented last year to defend against Microsoft Recall, Signal CEO Meredith Whittaker said similar measures have become necessary to prevent agentic software available in iOS and Android from gaining access to communication that's intended to be private. "Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems," wrote Whittaker in a blog post . "In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding." The result is that private messages ingested by these agentic systems may end up on someone else's server where they're no longer private. Updates to Signal's iOS and Android apps now include controls that by default block Siri on iOS and Gemini and other agents on Android from taking screenshots, which AI agents process using optical character recognition to extract text. Whittaker says that those who wish to take screenshots of their messages can disable this protection via Signal's settings menu, but warns doing so risks exposing your Signal content (and that sent by your contacts) to AI agents. Screenshot blocking, Whittaker concedes, is only a partial solution since AI agents may have other ways to access application data through the device file system. "We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy," she said. "Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS." Apple is taking some action to implement protection from AI agents on macOS, though it appears to be doing so largely to defend against third-party access to data rather than to limit its own Siri service. Siri can be turned off separately. With macOS 27.3 , currently in public beta testing, Apple's desktop operating system will get more granular controls on two APIs: Device Control and Data Access, and Full Disk Access. The result will be more permission prompts for users of macOS apps that seek access to user data, and the inconvenience of applying for an entitlement from Apple to obtain Full Disk Access for backup software and assistive technologies that use Accessibility APIs. "Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems," wrote Whittaker in a blog post . "In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding." The result is that private messages ingested by these agentic systems may end up on someone else's server where they're no longer private. Updates to Signal's iOS and Android apps now include controls that by default block Siri on iOS and Gemini and other agents on Android from taking screenshots, which AI agents process using optical character recognition to extract text. Whittaker says that those who wish to take screenshots of their messages can disable this protection via Signal's settings menu, but warns doing so risks exposing your Signal content (and that sent by your contacts) to AI agents. Screenshot blocking, Whittaker concedes, is only a partial solution since AI agents may have other ways to access application data through the device file system. "We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy," she said. "Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS." Apple is taking some action to implement protection from AI agents on macOS, though it appears to be doing so largely to defend against third-party access to data rather than to limit its own Siri service. Siri can be turned off separately. With macOS 27.3 , currently in public beta testing, Apple's desktop operating system will get more granular controls on two APIs: Device Control and Data Access, and Full Disk Access. The result will be more permission prompts for users of macOS apps that seek access to user data, and the inconvenience of applying for an entitlement from Apple to obtain Full Disk Access for backup software and assistive technologies that use Accessibility APIs. "As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially," Apple said when it introduced the Full Disk Access change. "We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy." Apple is also reportedly working on its own AI agent in a bid to compete with Anthropic and OpenAI. It remains to be seen whether Apple will use its operating system ownership as competitive leverage against AI firms that threaten its gatekeeping power, as it has done with web browsers . First the flood, then the dams While Apple casts itself as an ally that's helping to defend device customers against prying AI agents, Signal's decision to block Siri shows that AI agents have complicated trust decisions and the competitive landscape. AI agents are supposed to serve the user but when they spirit data away to the cloud and come between customers and merchants, they wear out their welcome. AI agents also threaten the business relationship between consumers and merchants. Amazon has blocked shopping agents like Meta Muse from its e-commerce site (though not AWS Marketplace ) while Walmart has invited third-party agents to interact through its AI Gateway. Anthropic has blocked subscription customers from using third-party harnesses . United Airlines has banned transactions from unauthorized AI bots. Similar barriers or limitations related to third-party AI agents have been erected by Target, Home Depot, Etsy, eBay, JPMorgan Chase, Charles Schwab, Citigroup, and Wells Fargo, among others. Meanwhile, there's a burgeoning industry in bot detection and mitigation, led by the likes of Cloudflare, Akamai, and DataDome, to name a few. The web browser is sometimes referred to as a user agent, based on the idealistic notion that it serves its user. That vision has been muddied by online advertising and data collection, and default settings that often serve the interests of browser makers instead of promoting privacy. Now AI agents face the same scrutiny as people wonder whether their agents really serve them or someone else. After a year or two of agent vendors arguing for access to all digital data for the sake of personalization and context, the backlash has arrived. ®

item.title: Watching as a giant star swallowed its neighbor and exploded
item.description: In the Andromeda Galaxy, a giant star about seven times as massive as the Sun spent nearly a decade slowly swallowing its much smaller companion. The process, known as common envelope evolution, was proposed in the 1970s to explain how some of the tightest pairs of stars in the Universe form, but no one had ever caught it in the act. In a new Nature study, astronomers led by Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University, finally witnessed the entire spectacle from the decades before it began to the eruption that ended it in late 2025. “It lasts for a few years, maybe a few decades,” Karambelkar said. “Stars evolve on time scales of millions of years. So, it's really like a blip on the entire cosmic time scale.” Shared envelopes Some pairs of stars orbit so close to each other that they could not have formed at that distance, so their orbits must have shrunk. Common envelope evolution is the leading explanation for that shrinkage. When one star in a binary grows old, it expands into a giant, and its outer layers can engulf its companion. The two then share a single, loosely bound envelope of gas. As the engulfed star drags through it, it loses orbital energy to friction and spirals inward. Depending on how much of the envelope gets lost, the pair either ends up in a much tighter orbit or merges. Read full article Comments

item.title: NASA’s new Moon plan is taking shape, but some big questions remain
item.description: SpaceX's successful recovery of its Starship rocket last weekend cleared a major hurdle on NASA's path to the Moon, opening up possibilities for higher launch rates and an all-important, long-delayed orbital refueling demo next year. For SpaceX's purposes, Saturday's mid-air rocket catch will help engineers learn how to rapidly reuse Starships. That should expedite SpaceX's deployment of its newest generation of Starlink Internet satellites. NASA, meanwhile, believes a higher launch cadence will lead to faster learning as SpaceX develops a deep space version of Starship to ferry astronaut crews to the surface of the Moon. Early next year, SpaceX plans to bring online a second Starship launch site at Kennedy Space Center, Florida. A second Starship factory is also under construction at Kennedy, joining SpaceX's existing SpaceX production line at Starbase, Texas. With two launch sites, SpaceX will have the pieces in place to take the next leap with Starship. Read full article Comments

item.title: Prisons get OK to jam contraband phones. CTIA says nearby phones will be jammed too.
item.description: The Federal Communications Commission yesterday voted to let state and local prisons use jamming technology to block contraband cellphones, despite warnings that jammers will also block lawful phone calls outside the prisons. Wireless industry lobby group CTIA said a recent test it conducted with the Virginia Tech Applied Research Corporation and South Carolina Department of Corrections confirmed concerns that the jammers would block legitimate communications, including 911 calls. CTIA told the FCC in an October 1 filing : The pilot test was limited in the number of micro-jammers deployed, the spectrum bands they were authorized to jam, and the power levels at which they were permitted to operate. Even with these constraints, the micro-jamming system blocked 911 calls, interfered with public safety and other communications, and caused interference that impacted wireless network infrastructure up to two and a half miles away. At the same time, the pilot results show substantial gaps in jamming the targeted “contraband” devices, with testing scenarios in outdoor inmate recreation areas showing failure rates—meaning “contraband” device call completion—in one-half to two-thirds of call attempts. CTIA said the pilot test shows "that current jamming technology seems to be both over and underinclusive at once—it risks blocking lawful communications even as it fails to block a significant portion of the targeted contraband device communications." Read full article Comments

item.title: Army delays detonating "catastrophically hazardous" lead azide amid fear, anger
item.description: In a swirl of questions, fears, and outrage, the US Army announced Thursday that it would delay a plan to blow up 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide, which would launch toxic gas and lead into the air. A federal appeals court further halted plans later on Thursday with an emergency order. The plume, containing neurotoxic lead, could potentially drift 100 miles north of the Army installation housing it in Middletown, Iowa, according to modeling released by the Army earlier this week. The Army had planned to carry out two controlled detonations, set off simultaneously around noon Friday, to destroy the barrels where they lie, which is in earth-covered concrete containment structures (called earth-covered magazines or ECMs). Prior to the court stay, the Army rescheduled the blast until November 23 to provide more time to communicate about the situation with Iowans, who have reported being unaware of the detonations until earlier this week. "Public communication is essential to public trust," Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a post on social media at 7:31 pm ET Thursday . "Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information." Read full article Comments

item.title: Eufy’s Omni C28 is 53 percent off ahead of Black Friday
item.description: Hosting Thanksgiving can be fun, but cleaning up afterwards? Not so much. Eufy’s Omni C28 robot vacuum / mop hybrid can help, and thanks to an early Black Friday deal, you can pick it up at a new low price of $379.99 ($420 off its original price) at Amazon , Best Buy , or directly from Eufy (with code WS24C28200NEW1 ) . While this model has dropped to around $499.99 a few times before, it commonly sells for a lot more, making now a great time to consider buying one. Eufy Omni C28 Where to Buy: $799.99 $379.99 at Amazon $799.99 $379.99 at Best Buy $799.99 $379.99 at Eufy (with code WS24C28200NEW1) The Verge’s smart home reviewer Jennifer Pattison Tuohy named the Eufy Omni C28 one of her top picks after testing 16 robot vacuum mops . She thinks it’s a particularly great fit for apartments and smaller homes. It offers features typically found in pricier flagship models, including a multifunction dock that automatically washes the mop roller with hot water and dries it with hot air, yet it doesn’t take up too much space. The robot itself is also relatively narrow and maneuvers easily around furniture and into tight spaces. It boasts excellent navigation, and had no trouble climbing over the legs of Jen’s lounger, which have tripped up many of the more expensive models she’s tested. The Omni C28 also does a great job cleaning with its mops, particularly on hardwood floors. Surprisingly, it’s powerful enough to lift up dried oatmeal. Unlike most other robot vacuums Jen’s tested, this one lacks a camera, making it a good option if you’re concerned about privacy. Unfortunately, the trade-off is mediocre obstacle detection, so you’ll want to pick up socks and cables before running it.

item.title: Nvidia’s journey to forge the one CPU SKU to rule them all
item.description: Each generation of Intel Xeons or AMD Epycs brings dozens of new SKUs: high-core count parts tuned for throughput, high-frequency ones optimized for latency, low-power chips designed for the edge, and everything in between. But if you ask Ian Finder, who heads development of Nvidia’s datacenter CPUs, for the vast majority of use cases, all those SKUs are overkill. “There was sort of an overskewing, for many years on the other vendors side of things,” he told El Reg on the sidelines of Supercomputing 2026 this week. Nvidia is a relative newcomer to the datacenter CPU space. The company’s first part, called Grace, launched in 2023, but didn’t see widespread deployment outside AI headnodes, high-end NICs, and a handful of standalone CPU deployments by hyperscalers like Meta. We explored the chip in greater detail earlier this year, but the GPU slinger’s latest CPU, Vera, is a different beast. In addition to showing up as part of Nvidia’s Vera-Rubin superchips, the CPU will also be offered in standalone CPU racks, storage, and context memory systems. Just this week, Nvidia announced a new rack with 192 Vera CPUs aimed at high-performance computing (HPC) workloads, which don’t translate well to GPUs. And at least on paper, a single SKU with 88 cores clocking to 3.3 GHz powers all of them. Historically, CPUs with different combinations of cores, clocks, I/O, and power have been used in these roles. According to Finder, most datacenter CPUs haven’t been loaded that heavily, and as a result unloaded latency has been the optimization point. As a consequence, CPUs that rely on high core counts to boost throughput often suffer from elevated loaded latencies. On the flip side, chipmakers can optimize for loaded latency, but this usually comes at the expense of throughput. We see this pretty clearly across AMD’s last few generations of Epycs, where it designed both space-efficient Zen-C cores that prioritize throughput and fatter frequency-optimized versions that prioritize latency. “As more cores are up and running, your latency to memory gets higher because you have to deal with congestion on the connectivity buses,” More than Moore analyst Ian Cutress tells The Reg . “What Nvidia is saying is right. Sometimes, you do have to pick between core count and core latency.” A balanced architecture With Vera, Nvidia sought to thread that needle to design a balanced architecture that maintains low latencies and high throughput even when all 88 cores are loaded. This does mean making some compromises – in particular, the CPU's vector unit isn’t the beefiest. But if you’ve got GPUs capable of running vectorized code, that compromise starts to make a lot more sense – and if you’re buying Vera you almost certainly do. “If you do a few things like that, you can actually get a part that, for the workloads people care about — knowledge agents for CI/CD, for software engineering, or databases and analytics — you can build a part that gets you the same performance per core
item.dc:creator: Tobias Mann
item.content:encoded: Each generation of Intel Xeons or AMD Epycs brings dozens of new SKUs: high-core count parts tuned for throughput, high-frequency ones optimized for latency, low-power chips designed for the edge, and everything in between. But if you ask Ian Finder, who heads development of Nvidia’s datacenter CPUs, for the vast majority of use cases, all those SKUs are overkill. “There was sort of an overskewing, for many years on the other vendors side of things,” he told El Reg on the sidelines of Supercomputing 2026 this week. Nvidia is a relative newcomer to the datacenter CPU space. The company’s first part, called Grace, launched in 2023, but didn’t see widespread deployment outside AI headnodes, high-end NICs, and a handful of standalone CPU deployments by hyperscalers like Meta. We explored the chip in greater detail earlier this year, but the GPU slinger’s latest CPU, Vera, is a different beast. In addition to showing up as part of Nvidia’s Vera-Rubin superchips, the CPU will also be offered in standalone CPU racks, storage, and context memory systems. Just this week, Nvidia announced a new rack with 192 Vera CPUs aimed at high-performance computing (HPC) workloads, which don’t translate well to GPUs. And at least on paper, a single SKU with 88 cores clocking to 3.3 GHz powers all of them. Historically, CPUs with different combinations of cores, clocks, I/O, and power have been used in these roles. According to Finder, most datacenter CPUs haven’t been loaded that heavily, and as a result unloaded latency has been the optimization point. As a consequence, CPUs that rely on high core counts to boost throughput often suffer from elevated loaded latencies. On the flip side, chipmakers can optimize for loaded latency, but this usually comes at the expense of throughput. We see this pretty clearly across AMD’s last few generations of Epycs, where it designed both space-efficient Zen-C cores that prioritize throughput and fatter frequency-optimized versions that prioritize latency. “As more cores are up and running, your latency to memory gets higher because you have to deal with congestion on the connectivity buses,” More than Moore analyst Ian Cutress tells The Reg . “What Nvidia is saying is right. Sometimes, you do have to pick between core count and core latency.” A balanced architecture With Vera, Nvidia sought to thread that needle to design a balanced architecture that maintains low latencies and high throughput even when all 88 cores are loaded. This does mean making some compromises – in particular, the CPU's vector unit isn’t the beefiest. But if you’ve got GPUs capable of running vectorized code, that compromise starts to make a lot more sense – and if you’re buying Vera you almost certainly do. “If you do a few things like that, you can actually get a part that, for the workloads people care about — knowledge agents for CI/CD, for software engineering, or databases and analytics — you can build a part that gets you the same performance per core as the frequency-optimized x86 parts at the same throughput per watt as the density-optimized parts,” Finder argued. We should note that Nvidia isn’t unique in this line of thinking. Cloud providers have long passed on the highest core-count parts in Intel or AMD’s lineup in favor of parts they feel deliver the right mix of throughput, latency, memory bandwidth, and capacity. The reason, in part, is that cloud providers don’t know exactly what their customers will actually be doing with those cores, and so it’s better to offer something that’s well-rounded than one that has the highest clocks or lowest latency. This same logic works pretty well for agent sandboxes. “Nvidia is confident that it understands the market well enough that one chip will cover most use cases,” Cutress said. “You could argue that Nvidia just wants to corner that bulk market.” Having said that, there are plenty of reasons to have multiple SKUs or product lines. Throughout much of AMD’s latest launch cycle, the House of Zen has argued its chips make for better agentic CPUs because agents aren’t one workload but many. Some may benefit from higher core counts while others may benefit from higher frequency, and AMD’s more diverse portfolio offers choice. To that point, Vera does have one trick up its sleeve: a split personality. The processor is one of the few Arm chips that supports simultaneous multithreading (SMT), but the way it works differs wildly from what Intel would call Hyperthreading. When enabled, SMT effectively bifurcates Vera’s Olympus cores. Eighty-eight cores turns into something that functionally looks more like 176 narrower cores. So if you need more throughput than 88 cores afford, or your workload doesn’t benefit materially from a wider core, Vera does offer some flexibility. A broader SKU stack also helps with binning. Chip manufacturing isn’t a perfect process, and you’re going to run into defective cores from time to time. Binning allows chipmakers to sell these defective chips at a discount. Cutress suspects that Nvidia is probably doing this for its customers and it’s just not advertising them as different SKUs the way Intel and AMD have the past few decades. For instance, a hyperscaler might be happy to take a 72-core variant of Vera that clocks a little higher or delivers more memory bandwidth per core for the same amount of power. But for now we have just the one, for the green lord on their green throne in the land of AI where the bots lie. ®

item.title: Multiplying your Switch 2’s storage costs less than usual right now
item.description: Expanding your Nintendo Switch 2’s 256GB of built-in storage with a microSD card is pricier than it was with Nintendo’s original console. That’s because microSD Express cards , while physically identical to ones you might have lying around, have faster read and write speeds. Thankfully, Samsung’s 256GB model has dropped to $44.99 at Amazon ahead of Black Friday, which is a few bucks off its usual price but still well below its $79.99 MSRP. Sandisk’s 256GB card, meanwhile, is available for $49.99 ($10 off Amazon’s typical list price) from Amazon and Sandisk , if you prefer one brand over the other for some reason. For those who don’t want to think about upgrading their Switch 2’s storage again, both brands’ 512GB microSD Express cards are selling for a fair $99.99 on Amazon . That gives you double the storage for roughly twice the price of a 256GB card, as it should be. Samsung P9 microSD Express Card Where to Buy: $79.99 $44.99 at Amazon (256GB) $149.99 $99.99 at Amazon (512GB) Sandisk microSD Express card Where to Buy: $166.99 $99.99 at Best Buy (512GB) $73.99 $49.99 at Amazon (256GB) $166.99 $98.99 at Amazon (512GB) I suspect the 256GB option will be enough for most Switch 2 players, unless you buy a lot of games. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is 24.9 gigabytes, for example. Other Nintendo-developed games tend to be similar in install size, though it’s all over the place for third-party game makers; Resident Evil Requiem (which also recently dropped to $39.99 on Amazon ) is relatively small at 28.7 gigs, while The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered is about 50. Some games take up even more storage.

item.title: ‘The greatest game ever made’: readers and Guardian staff on Grand Theft Auto VI
item.description: Rockstar’s newest installment of its hit franchise still has plenty of action, along with a dose of ‘healthy masculinity’ Described as the biggest entertainment launch in history, the new Grand Theft Auto game has prompted avid fans around the world to take the day off work, stock up on snacks and celebrate its arrival after 13 years of waiting. While some have already spent hours immersed in the game’s criminal escapades, others have found themselves doing household chores, building houses or simply taking in the scenery – which includes more than 170 flora and fauna species native to Florida . GTA VI has generated extraordinary global anticipation for its action-packed gameplay, but players are now finding new delight in the game’s more intimate moments. Continue reading...

item.title: Here are the Apple deals actually worth picking up ahead of Black Friday
item.description: A new pair of AirPods or the latest Apple Watch can make a great holiday gift, but they can also take a pretty big dent out of your budget. That’s especially true this year, as rising hardware prices have made MacBooks and other Apple devices even more expensive. Fortunately, Black Friday offers a chance to save, especially since great deals are already available on a wide range of Apple devices. Some discounts even extend to recent releases like the Apple Watch Series 12 and touchscreen MacBook Pro , which have dropped to new lows. Most of the discounts below are promoted as Black Friday deals, but we’ve also included a few that aren’t technically part of the shopping event but have “coincidentally” dropped in price in the last week or so. Black Friday isn’t until November 27th, however, so some prices could fall further in the coming days. Apple is also kicking off its own Black Friday shopping event that day, offering up to $300 in gift cards with select purchases. That said, if you don’t want to wait, we think the deals below are already worth taking advantage of. Earbud and headphone deals AirPods Pro 3 The latest AirPods Pro offer improved noise cancellation and richer bass, along with built-in heart sensors that work with Apple’s Fitness app to monitor calories burned across more than 50 workouts. Read our review. Where to Buy: $249 $179 at Amazon $249 $179 at Walmart $249 $179.99 at Best Buy Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 Beats’ fitness-focused earbuds feature ear hooks designed to stay put during even the most intense workouts as well as built-in heart rate monitoring. They also deliver relatively bass-rich sound for their design, along with solid noise cancellation, wireless charging, and AirPods features like adaptive audio thanks to Apple’s H2 chip. Read our review. Where to Buy: $249 $179.95 at Amazon $249 $179.95 at Walmart $249.99 $179.99 at Best Buy You can buy the AirPods 4 on sale at Walmart for around $89 ($40 off), which is $20 shy of their best price. Apple’s last-gen earbuds lack active noise cancellation, but they still deliver good, relatively bass-rich sound, even if they don’t quite match the newer AirPods 5. They also offer voice call quality on par with the latest AirPods Pro. Read our review . The second-gen AirPods Max are down to $419 ($130 off) at Amazon , which is $19 shy of their best price to date ( Best Buy and Target also have them for about $10 more). Like the original, Apple’s latest over-ear headphones feature a luxurious build consisting of aluminum, steel, and a mesh fabric, but they offer better sound and noise cancellation. The new H2 chip also enables features like adaptive audio and live translation. Read our review . Beats Studio Pro The latest Beats Studio Pro feature improved noise cancellation, sound quality, and comfort. They also support lossless audio over USB-C and offer native support for a range of iOS and Android features like other Beats headphones. Read our review . Where to Buy: $349.99 $139.95

Earbud and headphone deals AirPods Pro 3 The latest AirPods Pro offer improved noise cancellation and richer bass, along with built-in heart sensors that work with Apple’s Fitness app to monitor calories burned across more than 50 workouts. Where to Buy: $249 $179 at Amazon $249 $179 at Walmart $249 $179.99 at Best Buy Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 Beats’ fitness-focused earbuds feature ear hooks designed to stay put during even the most intense workouts as well as built-in heart rate monitoring. They also deliver relatively bass-rich sound for their design, along with solid noise cancellation, wireless charging, and AirPods features like adaptive audio thanks to Apple’s H2 chip. Read our review. Where to Buy: $249 $179.95 at Amazon $249 $179.95 at Walmart $249.99 $179.99 at Best Buy You can buy the AirPods 4 on sale at Walmart for around $89 ($40 off), which is $20 shy of their best price. They also offer voice call quality on par with the latest AirPods Pro. Read our review . The second-gen AirPods Max are down to $419 ($130 off) at Amazon , which is $19 shy of their best price to date ( Best Buy and Target also have them for about $10 more). Beats Studio Pro The latest Beats Studio Pro feature improved noise cancellation, sound quality, and comfort. item.title: China attackers deployed AI agents that autonomously found and exploited a 0-day to take over a university server
item.description: Suspected Chinese spies deployed AI agents which worked autonomously to find a zero-day in an open source application and then abuse the flaw to break into university networks, gaining full control of a server, according to Amazon CISO CJ Moses. The China-linked attacker used Cairn, an open source, penetration-testing framework that has become increasingly popular with cybercriminals who use the AI tool to carry out multi-stage intrusions with no human assistance . In this case, the agents found and exploited a zero-day MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging AI application. Amazon notified the project's maintainers of the vulnerability, and they released a fix and a security advisory . On September 10, Amazon's Threat Intelligence Team found a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn that provided visibility into the campaign targeting universities in East Asia, outside Mainland China, Moses said in a Friday report shared with The Register . The campaign occurred over a period of 48 hours beginning on September 8, and the prompts were written in Simplified Chinese, with timestamps in executed scripts configured to China Standard Time. Before the AI agents found and exploited the zero day, however, they tried to break into another university’s Redis server over about 16 hours and 148 sequential actions, including abusing Redis's replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory. None of these were successful, and when those actions failed, the agents also attempted a Log4Shell injection against a different service, a server-side request forgery (SSRF) attack against a vulnerability in a co-located Qdrant instance, and several credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH, and other tools. Meanwhile, a separate operation running for more than 6 hours targeted a university GPU server with another credential-spray attack, compiling a list of 80 real user names found across the school’s public websites, academic papers and other documents. "Neither operation succeeded, yet together they show that the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction," Moses wrote. Then the AI agents found the zero-day path traversal vulnerability in MONAI Label, and this time they were able to gain access to the server. "The agents identified the application's framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter," Moses wrote. They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server." Later, the agents abused the same flaw to execute a Python reverse shell running as root. In another session, after the agents discovered the zero-day, the human operator provided them with a proxy that tunneled into a second university network, and connected to a server running the same vulnerable

In this case, the agents found and exploited a zero-day MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging AI application. The campaign occurred over a period of 48 hours beginning on September 8, and the prompts were written in Simplified Chinese, with timestamps in executed scripts configured to China Standard Time. Before the AI agents found and exploited the zero day, however, they tried to break into another university’s Redis server over about 16 hours and 148 sequential actions, including abusing Redis's replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory. None of these were successful, and when those actions failed, the agents also attempted a Log4Shell injection against a different service, a server-side request forgery (SSRF) attack against a vulnerability in a co-located Qdrant instance, and several credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH, and other tools. Meanwhile, a separate operation running for more than 6 hours targeted a university GPU server with another credential-spray attack, compiling a list of 80 real user names found across the school’s public websites, academic papers and other documents. "Neither operation succeeded, yet together they show that the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction," Moses wrote. Then the AI agents found the zero-day path traversal vulnerability in MONAI Label, and this time they were able to gain access to the server. "The agents identified the application's framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter," Moses wrote. They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server." Later, the agents abused the same flaw to execute a Python reverse shell running as root. In another session, after the agents discovered the zero-day, the human operator provided them with a proxy that tunneled into a second university network, and connected to a server running the same vulnerable code. Amazon's discovery follows an earlier report by Gambit Security's threat intelligence team that also documented a Chinese operator using Cairn to carry out at least 105 attacks, and managing to compromise, "to varying degrees," at least 27 companies. This campaign also occurred in September. In addition to Cairn, the attacker used two other open source AI harnesses to steal credit card records and other sensitive data from a Fortune 500 hospitality company, a major US airline, a large private US industrial supplies distributor, and a US online fashion retailer, and other companies. "Together, these cases show that this autonomous AI agent framework is being adopted in both espionage and criminal operations," Moses wrote. ®

At home, just breathing makes the air more humid, let alone cooking or showering. And when it gets too humid, it’s bad for our health as well as our homes. In fact, the two are connected: humidity lets mould and dust mites flourish – and they, in turn, can trigger asthma and allergies. Continue reading...

item.title: Dutch data watchdog highlights safety issues with AI glasses
item.description: The Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) has officially advised consumers against buying AI-powered smart glasses after safety tests revealed concerning behaviors beyond their controversial recording capabilities. The AP recently tested six different models of smart glasses and found glaring issues, including a willingness to display dating advice to an adult glasses-wearer who expressed an interest in a minor. In another case involving a cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) simulation, testers noted that one pair of glasses informed the wearer that emergency services had been called and were scheduled to arrive at the scene, despite no one having made the call. Some glasses did not properly process safety warnings on children’s toys, others made mistakes when reading medication leaflets, and some misinterpreted warnings for extreme weather events. The AP did not specify the models it tested, saying only that they tested six models ranging from under €100 ($110) to over €500 ($550), including two that "were extensively tested in simulated real-life situations where human safety played a key role." A spokesperson also declined to match any specific behavior to a model by price point (minor dating advice linked to a €354 pair of glasses, for example), adding that the research was intended to highlight the risks of AI glasses in a broader sense. "Glasses that film you unnoticed are already concerning. Glasses that also give you incorrect advice when someone's life is at stake go a step too far," said Monique Verdier, vice chair at the AP. "AI offers many opportunities, but we must be able to trust that technology. With the camera glasses examined, that trust cannot currently be justified." The warning issued this week follows the regulator's previous work on smart glasses. The AP reminded the public in September that everyone has the right to privacy and encouraged organizations to ban them where necessary. The same warning mentioned the potential risks regarding data processing under the GDPR, as well as those related to the training of AI. The AP doubled down on these earlier criticisms, saying the latest tests showed that the AI functions rely on processing data using servers mostly located outside of the European Union. Relatedly, it found that users were not given sufficient information about how the AI was processing the data they captured. On a cybersecurity note, the tests threw up a range of issues, including the ability for people nearby the glasses-wearer to connect to the device without permission, view recordings, and in some cases operate the camera. Further, the regulator echoed the pre-existing concerns about smart specs - those that helped give them their colloquial name “pervert glasses.” Its tests found that with "virtually all of the camera glasses examined," the recording lights that are supposed to clearly show when a user is recording were dim and easily coverable. item.dc:creator: Connor Jones
item.content:encoded: The Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) has officially advised consumers against buying AI-powered smart glasses after safety tests revealed concerning behaviors beyond their controversial recording capabilities. The AP recently tested six different models of smart glasses and found glaring issues, including a willingness to display dating advice to an adult glasses-wearer who expressed an interest in a minor. In another case involving a cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) simulation, testers noted that one pair of glasses informed the wearer that emergency services had been called and were scheduled to arrive at the scene, despite no one having made the call. Some glasses did not properly process safety warnings on children’s toys, others made mistakes when reading medication leaflets, and some misinterpreted warnings for extreme weather events. The AP did not specify the models it tested, saying only that they tested six models ranging from under €100 ($110) to over €500 ($550), including two that "were extensively tested in simulated real-life situations where human safety played a key role." A spokesperson also declined to match any specific behavior to a model by price point (minor dating advice linked to a €354 pair of glasses, for example), adding that the research was intended to highlight the risks of AI glasses in a broader sense. "Glasses that film you unnoticed are already concerning. Glasses that also give you incorrect advice when someone's life is at stake go a step too far," said Monique Verdier, vice chair at the AP. "AI offers many opportunities, but we must be able to trust that technology. With the camera glasses examined, that trust cannot currently be justified." The warning issued this week follows the regulator's previous work on smart glasses. The AP reminded the public in September that everyone has the right to privacy and encouraged organizations to ban them where necessary. The same warning mentioned the potential risks regarding data processing under the GDPR, as well as those related to the training of AI. The AP doubled down on these earlier criticisms, saying the latest tests showed that the AI functions rely on processing data using servers mostly located outside of the European Union. Relatedly, it found that users were not given sufficient information about how the AI was processing the data they captured. On a cybersecurity note, the tests threw up a range of issues, including the ability for people nearby the glasses-wearer to connect to the device without permission, view recordings, and in some cases operate the camera. Further, the regulator echoed the pre-existing concerns about smart specs - those that helped give them their colloquial name “pervert glasses.” Its tests found that with "virtually all of the camera glasses examined," the recording lights that are supposed to clearly show when a user is recording were dim and easily coverable. The AP said that models could also be wangled into recording even when that light indicator was covered, which goes against what manufacturers so often claim. "As a result, bystanders can barely see whether they are being filmed," it said. The technology has a number of beneficial use cases, such as assisting the visually impaired, those with lower literacy levels, or for any number of other scenarios where people need help understanding the world around them However, the watchdog's official stance on the technology, as it is today, deems smart glasses "unsafe… due to the risks to users and bystanders." Verdier said politicians in the Netherlands and across Europe should take note of the results when developing AI policy. "It is important that we, as a society, learn to deal with these types of high-risk AI products," she said. "Simply banning everything provides some leeway in the beginning, but we cannot sustain that indefinitely. It is important that we collectively work on awareness, resilience, and ethical conscience." Smart specs can't shake the hate When DEF CON announced a no pervert glasses policy ahead of its event in August, the move was broadly welcomed by attendees. "Love to see a ‘no pervert glasses’ policy at DEF CON," said Eva Galperin, EFF director of cybersecurity, at the time. Several other organizations have implemented similar restrictions, including Monopoly Events, which manages UK Comic Cons, national treasure pub chain Wetherspoons , and even Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Most members of the general public will have at least come to terms with the fact that the smartphone generation, and their willingness to snap shots anywhere and everywhere, means there is no enshrined human right to privacy in public spaces. Public video recording once carried an air of expectation or consideration for bystanders’ personal privacy, although smartphone users have slowly eradicated that over time. Like it or not, it's generally understood that a smartphone is usually recording something - or someone - at any given time, especially in urban areas. On paper, the fact that smart glasses can record in public spaces isn’t wildly different from what’s already come to be expected from smartphones. However, given how similar they appear to analog glasses and the ability to cover the recording light, it makes the act of public recording via glasses far more surreptitious, and thus concerning. With smartphones, it's easy to see from the user's body language - holding the phone out in front of them - that they are recording. There are no overt signals displayed by wearers of smart glasses during image or video capture, which fuels a sense of unease about the technology in general. A quick search online for "smart glasses privacy violation" yields a slew of complaints about the technology, often regarding behavior toward women and children. There are also worries about how easily the devices can get past security checks, potentially providing opportunities to those who wish to cause greater harm than a mere blight on personal privacy. A joint investigation by The Observer and BBC Radio 4 recently revealed how AI-enabled glasses went undetected through the airport-style security scanners used in the UK parliament. The two news outlets found that a £60 ($78) pair of Chinese-made glasses bypassed the scanners and could be used to read upside-down documents on MPs' desks, recording data such as phone numbers and addresses to be accessed at a later point. ®

item.title: Valve says it might have to raise the price of supply-limited Steam Machines
item.description: When the Steam Machine first started shipping in June , Valve said it was producing fewer units at a higher price than initially planned because it couldn't secure supplies of scarce RAM and storage components at a reasonable cost. Now, as the last of the initial batch of Steam Machine reservations are finally being fulfilled, Valve says those supply and cost issues will continue into the foreseeable future and may even require a price change. "We are continuing to build more Steam Machine units, but memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels," Valve wrote in a blog post on Thursday . "As a result we don't yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price we'll be able to offer them. The 2TB model in particular will be especially constrained." If Valve does have to raise the price of the Steam Machine, it will be in good company. All three major console manufacturers instituted historically atypical price increases in 2025 , with additional price hikes happening this year. Read full article Comments
